site.lab_name: Synthetic Biology and BioProcess Engineering Lab
site.home_intro: The Synthetic Biology and Bioprocess Engineering Lab at Kyung Hee University (KHU) engineers microorganisms into cell factories for sustainable biomanufacturing. Our work runs along three connected lines. First, we build the foundational tools that make non-conventional hosts — methylotrophic yeasts, oleaginous microalgae, marine protists, and methanotrophs — as tractable as model organisms, developing CRISPR/Cas9 multiplex editing, in vivo DNA assembly, and safe-harbor expression systems. Second, we apply metabolic engineering to convert renewable carbon — CO<sub>2</sub>, methane, methanol, and lignocellulosic sugars — into three families of products: industrial chemicals and fuels (white biotechnology), pharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals (red biotechnology), and food and feed materials (green biotechnology). Third, we are building an AI-driven, automated design–build–test–learn platform, so that strain development becomes a data-driven and increasingly self-directed process rather than a manual one. Together these efforts aim at bioprocesses that are not only environmentally sound but economically competitive.

research.overview_sub:
Sustainable Synthetic Biology and BioProcess Engineering
for the Production of Value-added Products
research.intro: Fossil-fuel dependence and continuous greenhouse gas emission have made sustainable routes to fuels, chemicals, and materials an urgent research priority. Our answer is the microbial cell: given the right genetic tools and the right process, microorganisms can convert CO<sub>2</sub>, methane, methanol, and inedible biomass into products that are today made from petroleum. We organize this work into three research lines — the foundational tools that make new hosts engineerable, the metabolic engineering that turns them into producers of chemical, pharmaceutical, and food materials, and the automation and artificial intelligence that shorten the design cycle for both.

topics.title: Development of foundational synthetic biology tools for diverse microorganisms
topics.body: Synthetic biology begins with the ability to modify an organism at will, and for most industrially attractive microorganisms that ability is still limited. We develop the foundational toolkit that makes non-conventional hosts as tractable as model organisms: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing and multiplex integration, Golden Gate cloning, in vivo DNA assembly that bypasses E. coli cloning altogether, safe-harbor loci identified from transcriptional hotspots, RNAi-based knockdown, and transcription-factor engineering. Screening is built into the toolkit — fluorescence-activated cell sorting and high-throughput phenotype and genotype assays let us obtain desirable strains efficiently rather than one at a time. In Komagataella phaffii, for example, synergistic deletion of Ku70 with RAD52 overexpression raised integration efficiency from 15.3% to 68.1% with 50-bp homology arms, and enabled assembly of ten DNA fragments in vivo. We apply the same approach across methylotrophic yeasts, oleaginous microalgae, marine protists, acid-tolerant yeasts, and methanotrophs.

topics.title: Metabolic engineering for white, red, and green bioproducts
topics.body: With the tools in hand, the question becomes what to make. We direct carbon flux in engineered strains toward three families of products, following the colour convention of industrial biotechnology. White — industrial chemicals, fuels, and materials: organic acids such as lactic and malic acid, free fatty acids and their derivatives, and bioplastic precursors, produced from methanol, lignocellulosic sugars, and CO2. Red — pharmaceuticals and nutraceuticals: long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids including EPA and DHA, carotenoids, and terpenoids. Green — food and feed materials: microalgal biomass, single-cell protein, food-grade lipids, and natural pigments. The same feedstocks and the same host organisms serve all three; what differs is the pathway we install and the process we design around it. Representative results include 61.2 g/L malic acid from xylose, 67 g/L lactic acid without pH adjustment, EPA productivity of 14.4 mg L−1 day−1 in Nannochloropsis, and a 25% increase in DHA content in Schizochytrium.

topics.title: AI-driven automation: biofoundry and the self-driving lab
topics.body: Strain engineering is still largely manual, and the design–build–test–learn cycle is the rate-limiting step in biomanufacturing. We are building an automated, data-driven platform to shorten it: standardized genetic parts and assembly protocols that a liquid handler can execute, high-throughput cultivation and analytics that generate consistent phenotype data, and machine-learning models trained on that data to propose the next round of designs. Combined with genome-scale metabolic models and techno-economic analysis, the aim is a biofoundry in which the choice of the next experiment is made from data rather than intuition — a step toward a self-driving laboratory for microbial cell factory development.
